vignette:
Margaret

Margaret Chen was seventy-seven years old and had spent the last forty years studying watershed systems across the Pacific Northwest—work that demanded precision, patience, and an almost meditative attention to the slow movements of water through stone and soil. In March of last year, during a solo field survey in a remote canyon near the Columbia River, a man had emerged from the scrub oak as she was collecting samples. She had not heard his approach over the sound of the water. He had been methodical and quiet, and when it was over, she had walked back to her truck in a state of profound disconnection, as if her body had become a thing separate from her mind, something that had betrayed her simply by existing in the world.

The assault had shattered something fundamental in how Margaret understood safety. In the months that followed, she became convinced that what had happened was not random cruelty but a direct consequence of her own choices—the way she had dressed that morning, her decision to work alone, the fact that she had been absorbed in her data and not sufficiently vigilant. She had come to believe that you could never truly know who would harm you, that men carried an unpredictable danger, that her body itself was somehow complicit in the violation it had suffered. These thoughts moved through her mind with the weight of certainty, and they transformed the world into a place of constant threat assessment. Before entering any space—her office at the university, the grocery store, even her own home—Margaret found herself mentally mapping exits, identifying which doors opened outward, which windows might serve as escape routes if someone came too close. The act of planning escape had become as automatic as breathing, a vigilance that consumed her attention before she could even settle into a task.

This hypervigilance had begun to reshape her daily existence. When her colleague David had placed a hand on her shoulder during a department meeting to show her a data visualization, Margaret had flinched so sharply that the coffee cup beside her nearly overturned. Being alone with any man now triggered a cascade of physical responses—her heart accelerating, her muscles tensing, a desperate mental rehearsal of where she could run. She had started avoiding the open field sites entirely, confining her work to the laboratory where she felt the walls around her and could control who entered. Her supervisor had begun to notice her increasing absence from the field research that had always been the core of her identity. The rumination about how she might have prevented the assault had become relentless; she replayed the morning obsessively, imagining different choices—if she had worn different clothes, if she had brought someone with her, if she had simply stayed home. These endless loops of self-recrimination only deepened her conviction that the assault had been somehow her fault, that her judgment was fundamentally flawed, that she could not be trusted to keep herself safe.

The harder Margaret tried to protect herself, the more fragile the world became. She had stopped accepting hugs from her sister, had declined invitations to family gatherings where there would be men she did not know well. At night, she lay awake listening for sounds—the creak of a floorboard, the whisper of wind against the eaves—interpreting each noise as a potential intruder. Any sudden movement in her peripheral vision sent her into a state of acute alarm. The avoidance had metastasized into a kind of social isolation that only reinforced her sense of being fundamentally damaged, of her body being something shameful that needed to be hidden and protected. She had not been touched affectionately in nearly a year. It was this growing realization—that she had become a prisoner in her own life, that the assault had stolen not just a single afternoon but the texture of ordinary human connection—that had finally compelled her to call a therapist. Margaret was afraid that healing might mean accepting what had happened to her body, and she was terrified that it might not.
